title: Security projects: how do you get a control to everyone, and into IT projects before go-live?
short: Set a coverage target and dated exceptions before the pilot, run report-only first, and check every IT project at kickoff and before go-live.
answer: Before your next security rollout starts, write down its scope, a coverage target such as 98% of in-scope accounts enforced, and an end date for every exception, then run it in report-only or audit mode, a pilot and two or three rings. In the company's other IT projects, ask the security questions at kickoff and sign off before go-live, and scale the effort by protection need so only high-need projects wait for a full review.
audience: Heads of security, IT leads who own security, and project managers in small and mid-size companies

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: Define done in numbers before you start.
items.text: Count the scope from the inventory and set a target, such as 98% of in-scope devices in block mode by 31 March, with an exception cap. Count enforced, not deployed.

items.title: Watch before you enforce.
items.text: Keep a new Conditional Access policy in report-only mode for at least a week[^caplan]; it logs and blocks nothing[^careport]. Audit ASR rules first, except the standard protection rules[^asrtest].

items.title: Roll out in rings sized for your help desk.
items.text: Pilot with IT and a champion per business unit, then a representative ring, then everyone, in waves within your support capacity[^mfaplan].

items.title: Give every exception an end date.
items.text: Exclusion lists start short and grow[^caexcl]. Give each member of a policy's exclusion group a reason, an owner and an end date.

items.title: Ask security at kickoff, not before go-live.
items.text: The BSI requires involving the ISB early in larger projects and new applications and IT systems[^isms1]; Grundschutz++ lets you define when[^std3001].

blocks.title: Roll out a security change in this order

items.title: Who and what is in scope?
items.text: Count from the inventory, not the new tool; Defender's device discovery lists devices not yet onboarded[^discovery]. The security program sheet decides what goes first.

items.title: What would break?
items.text: Run report-only or audit mode for one to four weeks and review the results with app owners. For segmentation, allow and log first, as in the network segmentation sheet.

items.title: Who pilots it?
items.text: IT and a champion per business unit[^asrtest], with a channel for problems. What they hit becomes the user message and the help desk script.

items.title: When does the next ring start?
items.text: After a week with no open tickets. Reuse your Windows update rings if you have them.

items.title: When is it done?
items.text: When the tail is closed by name, the old path is gone, such as SMS codes, and an owner gets a monthly coverage report.

blocks.title: Users, help desk and rollback
items: **Tell users what changes, when, and how to get help**[^caplan], a week before their ring and on the day.
**Brief the help desk before each ring:** the script, known errors and what to collect, including the correlation ID from **More details**[^caplan].

**Write the rollback first:** the trigger and the switch. Disable the policy or exclude a group in Conditional Access[^caplan], add an ASR exclusion rather than return to audit[^asrtest], pause the Intune deployment[^intune].
**Exclude Mac, iOS and Android from report-only compliance policies,** or their users may get certificate prompts[^careport].
**In Germany, ask the works council early** about EDR, DLP and logging; it co-determines systems designed to monitor behavior or performance[^betrvg].

blocks.title: Exceptions that end
items: **Exclude groups, not people.** One assigned Entra group per policy shows who is excluded[^caexcl].
**Record why, what instead and until when:** a reason, a compensating control, an owner and an end date per member. Approval levels are in the risk register sheet.
**Let reviews remove people.** Entra access reviews can ask members weekly and remove those who don't answer (Entra ID P2 or ID Governance)[^caexcl].
**Cap them.** Our rule: at most 2% of the scope at go-live, none by the done date. Report the count and the oldest monthly.

blocks.title: Measure adoption against the inventory
items: **Coverage is enforced over in scope,** counted weekly from the inventory by ring and business unit, with the tail named.
**MFA and passkeys.** Entra's **Authentication methods** > **Activity** shows who is MFA or passwordless capable and single-factor sign-ins (P1 or P2)[^authact].
**Conditional Access.** The gap analyzer workbook lists sign-ins no policy applied to (P1 and Log Analytics)[^gap].
**EDR and ASR.** Compare onboarded with discovered devices in Defender[^discovery]. The ASR rules report needs Plan 2 or Defender for Business, or use event 1122[^asrtest].

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Stopping at 80%.** The tail holds old devices, service accounts, shared mailboxes and executives. Plan it as its own phase, with an owner per system.
**No owner after go-live.** Conditional Access policies have no owner field; Microsoft suggests naming the owner in the policy name and keeping a register[^caplan]. Do it for every control.
**Piloting only in IT.** IT and lab devices often lack the business apps and drivers that break[^rings].
**Reporting deployed as done.** A policy left in audit mode looks finished on the status page and blocks nothing.

blocks.title: Security gates in IT and business projects
items: **At kickoff, ask six questions:** what data, who signs in and how, internet-facing or not, which supplier, who gets admin rights, when it goes live.
**Rate the need: normal or high.** Grundschutz++ has just these two; only high needs an explicit risk analysis[^std3001]. Take 30 minutes with the business owner.
**Write requirements into the plan.** Normal: SSO with MFA, exportable logs, named admins, backups, patch deadlines. High: add a design review. Software you build: see the secure development sheet.

**Pentest before go-live** if it faces the internet, has high need, is custom-built or changes sign-in; ENISA expects tests at set-up[^enisatig]. Otherwise scan and check the configuration. See the penetration testing sheet.
**Sign off and hand over.** Security confirms each requirement or lists open items with owners and dates; management approves the risk of unmet ones[^std3001]. Name the operations owner.

blocks.title: Security in tenders and contracts
items: **Use the six NIS2 purchasing points:** security requirements, updates for the whole lifetime or replacement after support ends, component information, security functions and secure configuration, assurance, and how you validate it[^enisatig]. They bind digital providers; in Germany, BSIG § 30 requires security in acquisition of all NIS2 entities[^bsig30].
**Ask when support ends.** From 11 December 2027, the CRA requires manufacturers to state the month and year at the time of purchase[^craguide].
**Require free, prompt fixes,** tested and delivered as soon as an issue is known, as ENISA advises[^enisatig].
**Tie acceptance to evidence.** Make acceptance and the final payment depend on SSO and MFA working, logs flowing and critical pentest findings fixed. Add the third-party risk sheet's clauses.

blocks.title: Don't become the bottleneck
items: **Publish when security joins.** Grundschutz++ doesn't need the ISB active in every security-relevant project[^std3001]. Join the high-need ones.
**Promise a turnaround,** such as the operating model sheet's 5 working days. If you miss it, the project proceeds and records the open items.
**Pre-approve patterns:** a SaaS requirement set, a contract annex, a reference design.
**Put a champion in the PMO** to ask the kickoff questions and call you in for high-need projects.

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **A risk analysis for every project.** Grundschutz++ needs none for normal protection need, because its requirements already build one in[^std3001].
**A pentest before every go-live.** A standard SaaS app behind SSO needs a check of your tenant's configuration.
**Auditing the standard ASR rules.** Microsoft says they can go to block or warn without testing[^asrtest].
**Months in report-only.** A week to a month of real sign-ins shows the impact. Enforce, then fix the tail.

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **Intune stages policy rollouts.** Deployment plans, in public preview since September 2026[^intunenew], push Windows policies ring by ring and can be paused[^intune].
**Grundschutz++ wants a written project rule.** BSI-Standard 300-1 (20 October 2026) requires a security role in security-relevant projects and a rule for when[^std3001].
**The Commission clarified CRA support periods.** Its guidance of 27 July 2026 says five years is a floor, not a default[^craguide]. Ask for the end date in tenders now.

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: The IT lead or provider runs rollouts; a managing director approves exceptions.
Pilot with two or three users, then everyone.
Check IT purchases against the six NIS2 points.

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Write one page per rollout: scope, target, rings, rollback, exceptions, owner.
Report coverage weekly to the steering meeting.
Ask the kickoff questions in every IT project.

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: Ring by region or site, and hold mission-critical devices until last[^rings].
Make security sign-off a gate in the project method.
Put a security annex in every IT tender template.

changes.text: First draft, based on Microsoft Learn rollout guides, BSI ISMS.1 and Grundschutz++, and ENISA and Commission guidance.
